newsitem.title: UK: Gulf Canada flays Clyde forecast.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada flays Clyde forecast.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources persisted in a bitter takeover quarrel on Thursday, accusing target Clyde Petroleum of overstating its future potential to try to counter the 432 million pound ($699 million) bid.

Gulf Canada challenged the British company's technical analysis of a particular block from which the UK firm expects substantial crude flow by claiming its reserve risk has been "substantially understated".
The North American firm also questioned the development timing of North Sea block 9/14b and cast doubts over its future production rates.
"Clyde has almost certainly included a significant value for this project in its valuation, although the actual amount has been kept from shareholders," Gulf Canada said.
Clyde is contesting Gulf's bid offer of 105 pence per share, saying its net assets were actually valued at 120 to 144 pence per share.
Clyde's share price held firm at 116 pence on Thursday, reflecting hopes that Gulf Canada would raise the offer.
On February 4, Gulf Canada would have to either allow the current offer to lapse, extend the deadline of current price or raise the offer.
The predator had received acceptances for a mere 0.17 percent of Clyde's shares as on Monday.

Clyde has forecast an 18 percent rise in operating cash flow to at least 150 million pounds in 1997 with its production forecast to rise nine percent to an average 44,900 barrels of oil equivalent per day.
Clyde expects its production to grow to an average 55,200 boepd in 1998 and 60,200 in 1999.
Gulf says Clyde's forecast has been based primarily on the potential of North Sea block 9/14b.

Gulf quoted data from UK's Department of Trade and Industry and claimed there had been very limited delineation of the reservoir. "The substantial risk attached is not reflected in Clyde's view of reserves," it said.
Gulf also questioned the viability of transporting crude 20 kilometres to the Gryphon field, saying the heavy crude of 20 degree API and low reservoir pressure would require sub-sea pumps.
It also mentioned that the unconsolidated nature of the sand could hamper improvement in productivity. ($1=.6175 pound)
